spec: Given two dates date1 and date2 as (year, month, day) with date1 on or before date2, count the number of weekdays (Monday through Friday) in the half-open range starting at date1 (inclusive) and ending at date2 (exclusive), using the day-count-since-epoch approach to determine weekday.
Pad a string on the right with a given single-character fill string so its total length equals width. If the string is already at least as long as width, return it unchanged.

Return a list of (key, value) tuples for the k entries of d with the smallest values, ordered by value ascending and, for ties, by key ascending. If k exceeds the number of entries, return all of them in that order. If k is 0 or d is empty, return an empty list.
Given a valid Gregorian date (year, month, day), determine whether it falls on a Saturday or Sunday. Use Zeller's congruence to determine the day of week internally. Return True or False.
Replace every occurrence of the reserved Windows filename characters < > : " / \ | ? * with an underscore, then strip any trailing spaces or period characters from the end of the resulting name.
Compute (base raised to the power exp) modulo mod, for a non-negative exponent exp and a positive modulus mod, without necessarily computing the full power first.

Given two equal-length strings of '0' and '1' characters representing a step in a Gray code sequence, determine whether they differ in exactly one bit position. Return False if the strings have different lengths, contain any character other than '0' or '1', or differ in zero or more than one position.
Compute the number of trailing zeros in the decimal representation of n! (n factorial) for a non-negative integer n, without necessarily computing n! itself.
Convert a non-negative integer number of seconds into "HH:MM" (each field zero-padded to two digits) by rounding to the nearest whole minute, rounding exact half-minutes (30 seconds) up.

Write a function that finds the index i in a list of numbers that minimizes the absolute difference between the sum of the elements before index i and the sum of the elements after index i (the element at index i itself is excluded from both sums). If several indices tie for the minimum difference, return the smallest such index. Return -1 for an empty list.
Given a string s and a single character ch, return the index of the last occurrence of ch in s, scanning from the end. Return -1 if ch does not appear anywhere in s, including for an empty string.
Given a non-negative integer number of total minutes, return an (hours, minutes) tuple giving the whole number of hours and the remaining minutes (0-59).
Given a first name and a last name as separate strings, return them formatted as 'Last, First'.
Validate a dashed US phone number in the format 'XXX-XXX-XXXX' where the area code's first digit must be 2-9 (never 0 or 1) and all X's are digits. Return False otherwise.

Write a function that returns a new list with the elements at two given indices swapped, leaving all other elements unchanged. Assume both indices are valid for the list; the same index may be given twice, in which case the list is unchanged.
Given a string s, return a list containing the Unicode code point (ordinal value) of each character in s, in order. An empty string returns an empty list.

Given a date as (year, month, day) integers and an integer n (which may be negative), return the (year, month, day) tuple of the date n days earlier, correctly handling month and year boundaries and leap years.

Write a function that shifts the elements of a list to the right by n positions, dropping the last n elements and filling the first n positions with a given fill value; the result has the same length as the input. If n is 0 or negative, return a copy of the list unchanged; if n is at least the length of the list, return a list of the fill value repeated to the original length.

Given a string s, build and return a mask string of the same length where each character is replaced by a class marker: 'V' if it is a vowel letter (a, e, i, o, u, either case), 'C' if it is any other alphabetic letter, 'D' if it is a digit, or 'O' for anything else such as spaces or punctuation.

Given a starting weekday number (0=Monday .. 6=Sunday) and a non-negative count of consecutive days starting on and including that weekday, return how many of those days are weekend days (Saturday or Sunday).

Validate a checksum string of digits where the last digit is a check digit for the ones before it. Assign alternating weights +1, -1, +1, -1, ... (by position from the left, starting at +1) to the digits before the check digit, sum the signed values, and the check digit must equal that sum modulo 10 (Python's modulo, always non-negative). The body (all but the last character) must be non-empty and contain only digits. Return False otherwise.

Write a function that returns a list of prefix sums where each output element is the sum of all input elements strictly before that position (so the first output element is always 0). The output has the same length as the input; an empty input returns an empty output.

Write a function that returns the indices of all local maxima in a list: positions (excluding the very first and last index) whose value is strictly greater than both immediate neighbors. If the list has fewer than 3 elements, return an empty list.
Given a year and a full English month name (e.g. 'February'), return the number of days in that month for that year, accounting for leap years.

Validate a countdown timer string of the form 'HH:MM:SS' where each of the three fields is exactly 2 digits, hours can be any value from 00 to 99 (not limited to 23, since a countdown can exceed a day), and minutes and seconds must each be 00 to 59. Return False otherwise.

Given a time string in 'HH:MM' 24-hour format and an integer number of minutes to add (which may be negative), return a tuple (day_offset, new_time) where new_time is the resulting 'HH:MM' string and day_offset is the signed number of days the addition crosses (0 if it stays within the same day, 1 if it rolls into the next day, -1 if it rolls back into the previous day, and so on).

Validate a Markdown-style link string of the form '[text](url)'. The text inside the square brackets must be non-empty and must not contain ']'. The url inside the parentheses must contain no whitespace and must start with 'http://' or 'https://'. The entire string must match this pattern exactly with nothing before or after. Return False otherwise.

Validate a username string. It must be between 3 and 16 characters long (inclusive), start with an alphabetic letter, and every remaining character must be a letter, digit, or underscore. Return False for anything that violates these rules.

Word-wrap a string of space-separated words into lines of at most width characters (without splitting words, joining words in a line with single spaces), then prefix every resulting line with the given number of leading spaces, and join the lines with newlines. Assume no single word is longer than width.
visible_tests: assert wrap_indent_block('the quick brown fox', 10, 2) == '  the quick\n  brown fox'
assert wrap_indent_block('one two three four', 7, 0) == 'one two\nthree\nfour'

spec: Determine whether a positive integer n is a repunit: every decimal digit of n is 1.

Write a function that computes the running maximum from the right of a list of numbers: the i-th element of the result is the maximum of all elements from index i to the end of the list. Return an empty list for an empty input.

Given a starting integer day number, a non-negative integer n, and a tuple of weekday numbers (0=Monday .. 6=Sunday) treated as non-business days, return the day number reached after moving backward n business days from the starting day (the starting day itself is not counted).

Write a function that sorts a list of numbers in descending order (keeping duplicate values as separate entries) and returns the value at the second position (index 1) of that sorted order. Return None if the list has fewer than two elements.

Validate a dotted-quad subnet mask string: it must be 4 dot-separated decimal numbers each 0-255 (like an IPv4 address), and when the 32 bits are written out in order, all the 1-bits must come before all the 0-bits (a contiguous prefix of ones followed by zeros, with either extreme, all-zeros or all-ones, allowed). Return False if the format is invalid or the 1s and 0s are not contiguous in that order.
Given a fraction (for example 0.5 meaning fifty percent), format it as a percentage string with exactly one decimal place followed by a '%' sign, for example 0.5 becomes '50.0%'.
Wrap a string in double quotes, escaping any internal double quote characters with a preceding backslash before wrapping.

Given a string of whitespace-separated words, form an acronym by taking the first letter of each word, converting it to uppercase, and concatenating the letters together with no separators. An empty or whitespace-only string returns an empty string.

Given two strings a and b, interleave their characters one at a time starting with a: a[0], b[0], a[1], b[1], and so on. Once the shorter string runs out of characters, append the remaining tail of the longer string unchanged.

Join a list of strings into a natural-language list using commas, with 'and' before the last item but without an oxford comma. Zero items produce an empty string, one item is returned as-is, two items are joined as 'A and B', and three or more items are joined as 'A, B and C' with no comma before 'and'.
Given a dict d and a separator string sep, format each entry as 'key<sep>value' and return the resulting list of strings sorted alphabetically. An empty dict returns an empty list.
